solutions_list.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
solutions_list.clean_question_text: We measure best case time complexity of any algorithm by using (a) Θ(n) (b) θ(n) (c) O(n) (d) Ω(n) where n is the number of inputs.
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.family_title: Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis
solutions_list.clean_question_text: In which format(s) can we represent a sparse matrix (a) triplet format (b) CSR/YALE format (c) both (a) and (b) (d) none of these.
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
solutions_list.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
solutions_list.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

  <text x="175" y="46" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626" font-weight="bold">TOP →</text>
</svg>
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
solutions_list.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
solutions_list.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

solutions_list.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Write the pseudo-code for insertion sort. State its best-case, worst-case and average-case asymptotic complexity. (4 + 2) + (3 + 3) = 12
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.

solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
solutions_list.clean_question_text: State if the following statement is correct. Justify your answer. O(n²) = 2ⁿ²+100. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

solutions_list.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
solutions_list.clean_question_text: f(n) = 3n²+10n; g(n) = 2ⁿ³ ; then (a) g(n)  O(f(n)) (b) g(n)  Ω(f(n)) (c) g(n)  Ө(f(n)) (d) all of these.
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.

• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

solutions_list.clean_question_text: f(n) = 3n²+10n; g(n) = 2ⁿ³ ; then (a) g(n)  O(f(n)) (b) g(n)  Ω(f(n)) (c) g(n)  Ө(f(n)) (d) all of these.
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.

solutions_list.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.

• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
solutions_list.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
solutions_list.clean_question_text: If the base address of an array Z with dimension 10X20 is 2023 and the array elements are stored in column-major ordering, what will be the address of the element Z[10][15]? In case Z is stored using row-major ordering, what will be the memory address of the same element? [(CO1)(Understand & Remember/LOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
solutions_list.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Find the Big-Oh for T(n) = 48n¹⁰⁰+ 2ⁿ+2 + 3n² + 100. [(CO2)(Apply/IOCQ)] (6 + 1) + 3 + 2 = 12
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.family_title: Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Write a small C function (no need for main, header files etc.) to print the moves of the well-known Tower of Hanoi problem using recursion. Assume that the smallest disc is numbered as ‘disc 1’ and the largest is ‘disc n’. Each of the three pegs is represented by a char (datatype): source (‘S’), destination (‘D’) and temporary (‘T’). Given below are some examples of the moves that you will print: Move the disc # 12 from T to D Move the disc # 4 from S to T. [(CO3)(Understand/IOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.

solutions_list.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Find the Big-Oh for T(n) = 48n¹⁰⁰+ 2ⁿ+2 + 3n² + 100. [(CO2)(Apply/IOCQ)] (6 + 1) + 3 + 2 = 12
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

(a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Find the Big-Oh for T(n) = 48n¹⁰⁰+ 2ⁿ+2 + 3n² + 100. [(CO2)(Apply/IOCQ)] (6 + 1) + 3 + 2 = 12
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

Assume that the smallest disc is numbered as ‘disc 1’ and the largest is ‘disc n’. Each of the three pegs is represented by a char (datatype): source (‘S’), destination (‘D’) and temporary (‘T’). Given below are some examples of the moves that you will print: Move the disc # 12 from T to D Move the disc # 4 from S to T. [(CO3)(Understand/IOCQ)]
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

(a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.

solutions_list.clean_question_text: When does the worst case complexity happen for Insertion Sort? (a) When the array is already sorted (b) When the array is sorted in reverse order (c) When the array is not sorted (d) When the array is sorted till the midpoint and then reverse sorted
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.
