solutions_list.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Describe insertion sort with a proper algorithm. What is the complexity of insertion sort in the worst case? (8)
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

solutions_list.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
solutions_list.clean_question_text: Why do we use a symptotic notation in the study of algorithm? Describe commonly used asymptotic notations and give their significance. (8) 50
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
solutions_list.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

solutions_list.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

solutions_list.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
solutions_list.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
solutions_list.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].

• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

solutions_list.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

solutions_list.clean_question_text: Execute your algorithm for two passes using the following list as input: 66, 33, 40, 20, 50, 88, 60, 11, 77, 30, 45, 65 Describe the behaviour of Quick sort when the input is already sorted. (10)
solutions_list.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P186-PART2-Q177 (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
solutions_list.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
solutions_list.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
solutions_list.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
solutions_list.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
solutions_list.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
solutions_list.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
solutions_list.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: We measure best case time complexity of any algorithm by using (a) Θ(n) (b) θ(n) (c) O(n) (d) Ω(n) where n is the number of inputs.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.clean_question_text: In which format(s) can we represent a sparse matrix (a) triplet format (b) CSR/YALE format (c) both (a) and (b) (d) none of these.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-01-P01-Q01-sub-iii.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-vi.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-vi.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-vi.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-vi.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-vi.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-x.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-x.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-x.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-x.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-01-P02-Q01-sub-x.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-01-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-01-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-01-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-01-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-01-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.clean_question_text: Write the pseudo-code for insertion sort. State its best-case, worst-case and average-case asymptotic complexity. (4 + 2) + (3 + 3) = 12
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-01-P04-Q08-sub-b.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-01-P04-Q09-sub-b.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-01-P04-Q09-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-01-P04-Q09-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-01-P04-Q09-sub-b.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-01-P04-Q09-sub-b.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.

DOC-02-P01-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-02-P01-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-02-P01-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-02-P01-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? [(CO1) (Remember/LOCQ)] Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-02-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.clean_question_text: If for an algorithm, f(n) = 3n²+10, state the worst case asymptotic time complexity of the algorithm. Show that it follows from the definition of worst case asymptotic time complexity. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)] (1 + 3 + 2) + 3.5 + (0.5 + 2) = 12
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-02-P02-Q04-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: State if the following statement is correct. Justify your answer. O(n²) = 2ⁿ²+100. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)]
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-02-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-02-P03-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-02-P04-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-02-P05-Q08-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-02-P05-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-02-P05-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-02-P05-Q09-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-02-P05-Q09-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-02-P05-Q09-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-03-P01-Q01-sub-iv.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-03-P01-Q01-sub-iv.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-03-P01-Q01-sub-iv.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-03-P01-Q01-sub-iv.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-03-P01-Q01-sub-iv.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: f(n) = 3n²+10n; g(n) = 2ⁿ³ ; then (a) g(n)  O(f(n)) (b) g(n)  Ω(f(n)) (c) g(n)  Ө(f(n)) (d) all of these.
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-03-P02-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-03-P03-Q06-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-04-P01-Q01-sub-iv.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-04-P01-Q01-sub-iv.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-04-P01-Q01-sub-iv.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-04-P01-Q01-sub-iv.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.

DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: f(n) = 3n²+10n; g(n) = 2ⁿ³ ; then (a) g(n)  O(f(n)) (b) g(n)  Ω(f(n)) (c) g(n)  Ө(f(n)) (d) all of these.
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-04-P02-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-04-P03-Q06-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-05-P01-Q01-sub-iv.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-05-P01-Q01-sub-iv.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-05-P01-Q01-sub-iv.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-05-P01-Q01-sub-iv.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-05-P01-Q01-sub-iv.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: f(n) = 3n²+10n; g(n) = 2ⁿ³ ; then (a) g(n)  O(f(n)) (b) g(n)  Ω(f(n)) (c) g(n)  Ө(f(n)) (d) all of these.
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-05-P02-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-05-P03-Q06-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-06-P02-Q01-sub-xi.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-06-P02-Q01-sub-xi.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-06-P02-Q01-sub-xi.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-06-P02-Q01-sub-xi.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-06-P02-Q01-sub-xi.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-06-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-06-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-06-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-06-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.clean_question_text: If the base address of an array Z with dimension 10X20 is 2023 and the array elements are stored in column-major ordering, what will be the address of the element Z[10][15]? In case Z is stored using row-major ordering, what will be the memory address of the same element? [(CO1)(Understand & Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-06-P02-Q03-sub-b.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-06-P03-Q07-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-06-P03-Q07-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].

DOC-07-P02-Q01-sub-xi.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-07-P02-Q01-sub-xi.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-07-P02-Q01-sub-xi.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-07-P02-Q01-sub-xi.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-07-P02-Q01-sub-xi.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-07-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-07-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-07-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-07-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-07-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

In case Z is stored using row-major ordering, what will be the memory address of the same element? [(CO1)(Understand & Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-07-P02-Q03-sub-b.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-07-P03-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-07-P03-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-07-P03-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-07-P03-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-07-P03-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-07-P03-Q07-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-07-P04-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.

DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-08-P02-Q01-sub-xii.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-08-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-08-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-08-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-08-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-08-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.clean_question_text: If the base address of an array Z with dimension 10X20 is 2023 and the array elements are stored in column-major ordering, what will be the address of the element Z[10][15]? In case Z is stored using row-major ordering, what will be the memory address of the same element? [(CO1)(Understand & Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-08-P02-Q03-sub-b.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-08-P03-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-08-P03-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-08-P03-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-08-P03-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-08-P03-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-08-P03-Q07-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-08-P03-Q07-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-08-P03-Q07-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-08-P03-Q07-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-08-P03-Q07-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-09-P02-Q01-sub-xi.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: Prove: n² + 100 n = θ(n²). [(CO1)(Understand and Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.clean_question_text: If the base address of an array Z with dimension 10X20 is 2023 and the array elements are stored in column-major ordering, what will be the address of the element Z[10][15]? In case Z is stored using row-major ordering, what will be the memory address of the same element? [(CO1)(Understand & Remember/LOCQ)]
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-09-P02-Q03-sub-b.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-09-P03-Q07-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: Let A be a two-dimensional array declared as follows: A: array [1…10] [1…15] of character; Assuming that each character takes one memory locations the array is stored in row-major order and the first element of the array is stored in location 100, what is the address of the element A[i][j] ? (a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-viii.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-viii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-viii.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-viii.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-10-P01-Q01-sub-viii.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.
