DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.clean_question_text: If the number of nonzero elements in the triple representation of a sparse matrix of m × n dimension is K, then what is the time complexity to read an element from the index [i][j] of the sparse matrix. Assume that the sparse matrix is stored in triple format. [(CO4)(Analyze/LOCQ)]
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-10-P02-Q02-sub-b.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-10-P02-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.family_title: Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.clean_question_text: Write a small C function (no need for main, header files etc.) to print the moves of the well-known Tower of Hanoi problem using recursion. Assume that the smallest disc is numbered as ‘disc 1’ and the largest is ‘disc n’. Each of the three pegs is represented by a char (datatype): source (‘S’), destination (‘D’) and temporary (‘T’). Given below are some examples of the moves that you will print: Move the disc # 12 from T to D Move the disc # 4 from S to T. [(CO3)(Understand/IOCQ)]
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-10-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-10-P03-Q08-sub-c.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-viii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-11-P01-Q01-sub-viii.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.

DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-11-P02-Q02-sub-b.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-11-P02-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-11-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-11-P03-Q08-sub-c.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

(a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-12-P01-Q01-sub-viii.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-12-P02-Q01-sub-xv.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-12-P02-Q01-sub-xv.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-12-P02-Q01-sub-xv.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-12-P02-Q01-sub-xv.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-12-P02-Q01-sub-xv.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-12-P02-Q02-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:

• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).

DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-12-P02-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.family_title: Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.clean_question_text: Write a small C function (no need for main, header files etc.) to print the moves of the well-known Tower of Hanoi problem using recursion. Assume that the smallest disc is numbered as ‘disc 1’ and the largest is ‘disc n’. Each of the three pegs is represented by a char (datatype): source (‘S’), destination (‘D’) and temporary (‘T’). Given below are some examples of the moves that you will print: Move the disc # 12 from T to D Move the disc # 4 from S to T. [(CO3)(Understand/IOCQ)]
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-12-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-12-P03-Q08-sub-c.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: Let A be a two-dimensional array declared as follows: A: array [1…10] [1…15] of character; Assuming that each character takes one memory location, the array is stored in row-major order and the first element of the array is stored in location 100, what is the address of the element A[i][j] ? DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: When does the worst case complexity happen for Insertion Sort? (a) When the array is already sorted (b) When the array is sorted in reverse order (c) When the array is not sorted (d) When the array is sorted till the midpoint and then reverse sorted
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-13-P01-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-13-P02-Q02-sub-c.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-13-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-13-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-13-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-13-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-13-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-13-P02-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-13-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-13-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-13-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-13-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: Let A be a two-dimensional array declared as follows: A: array [1…10] [1…15] of character; Assuming that each character takes one memory location, the array is stored in row-major order and the first element of the array is stored in location 100, what is the address of the element A[i][j] ? (a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: When does the worst case complexity happen for Insertion Sort? (a) When the array is already sorted (b) When the array is sorted in reverse order (c) When the array is not sorted (d) When the array is sorted till the midpoint and then reverse sorted
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-14-P01-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-14-P02-Q02-sub-c.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-14-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-14-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-14-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-14-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-14-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-14-P02-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-14-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-14-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-14-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-14-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: Let A be a two-dimensional array declared as follows: A: array [1…10] [1…15] of character; Assuming that each character takes one memory location, the array is stored in row-major order and the first element of the array is stored in location 100, what is the address of the element A[i][j] ? (a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: When does the worst case complexity happen for Insertion Sort? (a) When the array is already sorted (b) When the array is sorted in reverse order (c) When the array is not sorted (d) When the array is sorted till the midpoint and then reverse sorted
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-15-P01-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-15-P02-Q02-sub-c.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-15-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-15-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-15-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-15-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-15-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-15-P02-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-15-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-15-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-15-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-15-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: Let A be a two-dimensional array declared as follows: A: array [1…10] [1…15] of character; Assuming that each character takes one memory location, the array is stored in row-major order and the first element of the array is stored in location 100, what is the address of the element A[i][j] ? (a) 15i + j + 84 (b) 15j + i + 84 (c) 10i + j + 89 (d) 10j + i + 89
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-16-P01-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.family_title: Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-16-P02-Q02-sub-c.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-16-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-16-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-16-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-16-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-16-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-16-P02-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-16-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-16-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-16-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-16-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-18-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.clean_question_text: The running time of an algorithm, T(n), where ‘n’ is the input size, is given by T(n) = 1, for n = 1 and T(n) = T(n/3) + c, for n > 1. Find the order of the algorithm.
DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-18-P03-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.

DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-b.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.

DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-18-P03-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-b.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-b.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-18-P05-Q08-sub-b.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-19-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-19-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-19-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-19-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-iii.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-iii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-iii.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-iii.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-iii.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-19-P02-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? [(CO1) (Remember/LOCQ)] Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-19-P03-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.
