DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.clean_question_text: If for an algorithm, f(n) = 3n²+10, state the worst case asymptotic time complexity of the algorithm. Show that it follows from the definition of worst case asymptotic time complexity. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)] (1+3+2) + (3.5) + (0.5 + 2) = 12
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-19-P04-Q04-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: State if the following statement is correct. Justify your answer. O(n²) = 2ⁿ²+100 [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)]
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-19-P05-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-19-P08-Q05-sub-b.family_title: Stack implementation using array and linked list, overflow and underflow conditions
DOC-19-P08-Q05-sub-b.clean_question_text: Why is a Tail recursive function more efficient compared to a normal recursive function? Ans. It is because the spaces of the local variables defined in the first call can be reused in every call as the scope of those variables of the earlier call ends before the next call is made. This is so because the recursive call is the last call in the function and hence the variable instances of the earlier call cannot be used after the next call is made. This saves a significant amount of overhead that is otherwise required whenever a function call is made. [(CO1) (Remember/LOCQ)]

DOC-19-P13-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-19-P13-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-19-P13-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-19-P13-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-19-P13-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.clean_question_text: i) Suppose you are performing an insertion sort on the following elements stored in an array. 22, 29, 35, 42, 39, 25, 15, 32, 29 What will be the total number of comparisons required to sort them in ascending order? It is better to list the number of comparisons suffered by each element so that you may get some marks even if you do any mistake in evaluating the total count. ANS. - 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 5 = 25 comparisons among array elements. [(CO6) (Evaluate/IOCQ)]
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-19-P14-Q09-sub-c.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.

DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.family_title: Binary Search: algorithm, mid element calculation, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.clean_question_text: Do an average case analysis for finding the time complexity of Binary Search. Assume that the element you are trying to find is there in the array, i.e., the probability of not finding the element is zero. [(CO6) (Analyze/IOCQ)] ANS. • Suppose when you first compare the key with the middle element, it matches, then the number of comparisons required to find the key is only 1. Number of positions for which only one comparison is required is therefore 1. • Now if you do not find the key in the 1st comparison but you find it in the 2ⁿd comparison, then number of such positions = 2 (middle elements of the half-arrays). • The number of positions for which 3 comparisons are reqd. is 4. • Hence average number of comparisons • ≤ (1/n) [(1.1 + 2.2 + 4.3 + 8. 4 + …+ 2 (lgn - 1) lgn)] = S / n (say) S = 1.1 + 2.2 + 4.3 + 8. 4 + … + 2 (lgn - 1) lgn) 2S = 2.1 + 4.2 + 8.3 + 16.4 +………………..+ 2lgn lgn S - 2S = 1 + [2(2-1) + 4(3-2) + 8(4-3) + ………] - 2lgn lgn -S = 1 + [2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + …. + 2 (lgn - 1) ] - 2lgn lgn -S = 1 + [2(2 (lgn - 1) -1) / (2 -1)] - n lgn = 1 + 2(n/2 - 1) - n lg n = 1 + n - 2 - n lg n So, S = n lg n - n + 1. So, Tavg(n) = (n lg n - n + 1)/n = lg n - 1 + 1/n = O(lg n)

DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.time_complexity: Best Case: O(1), Worst Case: O(log n), Average Case: O(log n)
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.space_complexity: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive call stack
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-19-P15-Q09-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-19-P16-Q02.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-19-P16-Q02.clean_question_text: k-1 T(n/2 k-1) = 2kT(n/2k) + cn = 2kT(1) + cn = cn, considering 2 k-1 < n ≤ 2k. Adding all, we get T(n) = cnk ≤ c n lg n = O(n lg n)
DOC-19-P16-Q02.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-19-P16-Q02 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-19-P16-Q02.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-19-P16-Q02.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-19-P16-Q02.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-19-P16-Q02.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-19-P16-Q02.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: In a 2D array int arr[100][50], the base address is 100. Then what will be the address of arr[50][30]? (a) 5162 (b) 5160 (c) 5100 (d) None of these

DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-iii.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-iii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-iii.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-iii.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-iii.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.clean_question_text: Linked Lists are not suitable for implementing (a) Insertion Sort (b) Binary Search (c) Linear Search (d) Selection Sort
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-20-P01-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-20-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-b.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-b.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-b.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.clean_question_text: If for an algorithm, f(n) = 3n²+10, state the worst case asymptotic time complexity of the algorithm. Show that it follows from the definition of worst case asymptotic time complexity. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)] (1 + 3 + 2) + 3.5 + (0.5 + 2) = 12
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-20-P02-Q04-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: State if the following statement is correct. Justify your answer. O(n²) = 2ⁿ²+100. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)]
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-20-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.clean_question_text: Given a 2D matrix of dimension 100 x 200 and also given that the base address of the 2D array is 2020. Assume that the array index of the matrix starts from [10, 20]. Find the address of the element with index [50,160] for column major ordering. [(CO2) (Understand/IOCQ)]
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-20-P03-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-20-P04-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-20-P04-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-20-P04-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-20-P04-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-20-P04-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.clean_question_text: (i) Suppose you are performing an insertion sort on the following elements stored in an array. 22, 29, 35, 42, 39, 25, 15, 32, 29 What will be the total number of comparisons required to sort them in ascending order? [(CO6) (Evaluate/IOCQ)] (ii) Suppose in a certain type of search in an array of size n, after each comparison of the target with an array element, the search space becomes approximately cube root of n and after exactly k comparisons the search space reduces to 2 elements. What will be the asymptotic time complexity? [(CO1) (Analyze/HOCQ)] (3 + 1 + 2) + 2 + (2 + 2) = 12
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-20-P05-Q08-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-20-P05-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-20-P05-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-20-P05-Q09-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-20-P05-Q09-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-20-P05-Q09-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.clean_question_text: We measure best case time complexity of any algorithm by using (a) Θ(n) (b) θ(n) (c) O(n) (d) Ω(n) where n is the number of inputs.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-i.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iii.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iii.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iii.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iii.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iv.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iv.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iv.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-21-P01-Q01-sub-iv.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.clean_question_text: Tower of Hanoi problem can be solved in (a) O(n) (b) O(n^2) (c) O(nlogn) (d) O(2^n) time, when n= Number of disks
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-ix.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-x.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-x.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-x.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-x.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-21-P02-Q01-sub-x.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-21-P03-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-21-P03-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-21-P03-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-21-P03-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-21-P03-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.clean_question_text: Write the pseudo-code for insertion sort. State its best-case, worst-case and average-case asymptotic complexity. (4 + 2) + (3 + 3) = 12
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-21-P04-Q08-sub-b.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-21-P04-Q09-sub-b.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-21-P04-Q09-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-21-P04-Q09-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:

• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).

DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.clean_question_text: The running time of a linear time algorithm is (a) O(1) (b) O(n) (c) O(n log n) (d) O(log n)
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-v.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.clean_question_text: What is not true about insertion sort? (a) Exhibits the worst case performance when the initial array is sorted in reverse order.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-22-P01-Q01-sub-vii.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-22-P02-Q01-sub-viii.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-22-P02-Q01-sub-viii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-22-P02-Q01-sub-viii.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.

DOC-22-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-22-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-22-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.

• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.

DOC-22-P02-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-22-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-22-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-22-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-22-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-22-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-22-P03-Q05-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-22-P03-Q05-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-22-P03-Q05-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-22-P03-Q05-sub-a.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-22-P03-Q05-sub-a.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-22-P04-Q08-sub-b.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-22-P04-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-22-P04-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).

DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.clean_question_text: The running time of a linear time algorithm is (a) O(1) (b) O(n) (c) O(n log n) (d) O(log n)
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-v.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.clean_question_text: What is not true about insertion sort? (a) Exhibits the worst case performance when the initial array is sorted in reverse order.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-23-P01-Q01-sub-vii.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-23-P02-Q01-sub-viii.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-23-P02-Q01-sub-viii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-23-P02-Q01-sub-viii.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.

DOC-23-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-23-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-23-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-23-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-23-P02-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-23-P02-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-23-P02-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-23-P02-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-23-P02-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-23-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-23-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-23-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-23-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-23-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-23-P03-Q05-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-23-P03-Q05-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-23-P03-Q05-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-23-P03-Q05-sub-a.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-23-P03-Q05-sub-a.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-23-P04-Q08-sub-b.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-b.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:

• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-23-P04-Q09-sub-b.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.

DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-ii.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-ii.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.clean_question_text: Which notation provides a strict lower bound for f(n)? (a) Omega (b) Big O (c) Small o (d) Theta.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-25-P01-Q01-sub-vi.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-25-P02-Q02-sub-b.step_by_step_explanation:

5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-25-P02-Q02-sub-b.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).

DOC-25-P02-Q04-sub-a.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-25-P02-Q04-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-25-P02-Q04-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-25-P02-Q04-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-25-P02-Q04-sub-a.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-25-P02-Q05-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-25-P02-Q05-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-25-P02-Q05-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-25-P02-Q05-sub-a.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-25-P02-Q05-sub-a.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-25-P03-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-25-P03-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-25-P03-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-25-P03-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-25-P03-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-ii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-ii.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-ii.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.

DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-iii.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-iii.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-iii.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-iii.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-iii.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.clean_question_text: Linked Lists are not suitable for implementing (a) Insertion Sort (b) Binary Search (c) Linear Search (d) Selection Sort
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-26-P01-Q01-sub-v.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.
