DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.clean_question_text: What is a sparse matrix? [(CO1) (Remember/LOCQ)] Given the following 4 × 5 matrix: 0 0 6 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a (Sparse matrix 3-tuple / triplet representation and memory benefit analysis)
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.time_complexity: O(k) where k is number of non-zero elements
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.direct_answer: Stored as a 3-tuple array [Row, Column, Value] with header row [m, n, k].
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Scan the matrix of dimensions m × n.
2. Count non-zero elements = k.
3. Row 0 of triplet array stores: [Total Rows m, Total Cols n, Total Non-Zero k].
4. Subsequent rows 1 to k store: [row_idx, col_idx, value] in row-major order.
5. Memory Benefit Check: Regular matrix uses m × n × w bytes. Triplet array uses 3 × (k + 1) × w bytes. Beneficial when 3(k+1) < m·n.
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Triplet Format: (Row, Column, Value).
• Row 0: Header storing (Total Rows, Total Columns, Total Non-Zero elements).
• Rows 1..k: Non-zero entries listed in ascending row-major order.
• Justification: Memory saved when 3·(k + 1) < m · n (i.e. non-zero elements < 33%).
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.common_mistakes: Omitting the header row (row 0), or listing coordinates in random rather than sorted order.
DOC-26-P02-Q02-sub-a.beginner_notes: Header row tells you the original matrix size so you can reconstruct it.

• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.

DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.clean_question_text: If for an algorithm, f(n) = 3n²+10, state the worst case asymptotic time complexity of the algorithm. Show that it follows from the definition of worst case asymptotic time complexity. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)] (1 + 3 + 2) + 3.5 + (0.5 + 2) = 12
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.direct_answer: Asymptotic bound verified mathematically using formal definition.
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Identify given function f(n) and candidate bounding function g(n).
2. For polynomial f(n) = a·n^k + ... + c, replace lower order terms with n^k for n ≥ 1.
3. Upper bound: f(n) ≤ (sum of absolute coefficients) · n^k = c2 · g(n).
4. Lower bound: f(n) ≥ a · n^k = c1 · g(n) for n ≥ 1.
5. Since c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) holds for all n ≥ 1, f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Given: Function f(n).
• Upper Bound Analysis: Choose c2 such that f(n) ≤ c2·n^k for n ≥ n0.
• Lower Bound Analysis: Choose c1 such that c1·n^k ≤ f(n) for n ≥ n0.
• Result: Both bounds hold for positive constants c1, c2, n0. Therefore f(n) = Θ(g(n)).
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-26-P02-Q04-sub-c.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.clean_question_text: State if the following statement is correct. Justify your answer. O(n²) = 2ⁿ²+100. [(CO1) (Apply/IOCQ)]
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-26-P02-Q03-sub-a.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

Assume that the array index of the matrix starts from [10, 20]. Find the address of the element with index [50,160] for column major ordering. [(CO2) (Understand/IOCQ)]
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-26-P03-Q03-sub-c.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-26-P04-Q08-sub-a.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

What will be the asymptotic time complexity? [(CO1) (Analyze/HOCQ)] (3 + 1 + 2) + 2 + (2 + 2) = 12
DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-26-P05-Q08-sub-c.exam_ready_answer:

• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.

DOC-26-P05-Q09-sub-a.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-26-P05-Q09-sub-a.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-26-P05-Q09-sub-a.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-26-P05-Q09-sub-a.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.
DOC-26-P05-Q09-sub-a.beginner_notes: Each comparison cuts the search space in half. 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };

DOC-30-P01-Q03.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-30-P01-Q03.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-30-P01-Q03.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-30-P01-Q06.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-30-P01-Q06.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If operator op: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (strict > if right-associative ^), pop and append to output; then push op.
3. At end of input, pop and append all remaining operators from stack.
DOC-30-P01-Q06.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-30-P01-Q06.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.
DOC-30-P01-Q06.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-30-P04-Q16.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-30-P04-Q16.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-30-P04-Q16.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-30-P04-Q16.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-30-P04-Q16.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-30-P04-Q16.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-30-P08-Q31.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
DOC-30-P08-Q31.clean_question_text: Consider the linear arrays AAA(5:50), BBB (-5:10) and CCC(18). (a) Find the number of elements in each array (b) Suppose Base(AAA) = 300 and w=4 words per memory cell for AAA. Find the address of AAA[15], AAA[35] and AAA[55] Ans : (a) Length = Upper Bound (UB) - Lower Boun d (LB) +1 Length(AAA) = 50-5+1 = 46 Length(BBB) = 10-(-5)+1 = 16 Length(CCC) = 18-1+1 = 18 (b) Using the formula: LOC(AAA[k]) = Base(AAA)+w(K- LB) LOC(AAA[15] )= 300+4(15-5) = 340 LOC(AAA[35] )= 300+4(35-5) = 420 AAA[55] is not an element of AAA since 55 exceeds UB = 50.
DOC-30-P08-Q31.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-30-P08-Q31 (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-30-P08-Q31.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-30-P08-Q31.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-30-P08-Q31.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-30-P08-Q31.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-30-P08-Q31.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-30-P09-Q34.beginner_notes: Operands never touch the stack; only operators and parentheses enter the stack.

DOC-30-P12-Q59.family_title: Bubble Sort: algorithm, step-by-step pass trace, and early termination optimization
DOC-30-P12-Q59.clean_question_text: Explain bubble sort. Ans : It requires n-1 passes to sort an array.  In each pass every element a[i] is compared with a[i+1], for i=0 to (n-k-1), where k is the pass number and if they are out of order i.e. if a[i]>a[i+1], they are swapped.   This will cause the largest element to move up or bubble up.    Thus after the end of the first pass the largest element in the array will be placed in the last or nth position and on the next pass, the next largest element will be placed at position (n-1). This continues for each successive pass until the last or (n-1)th pass when the second smallest element will be placed at the second position.  Pass1. Step 1. if a[0]>a[1] then swap a[0] and a[1]. Step 2. if a[1]>a[2] then swap a[1] and a[2]. … Step n-1. if a[n-2]>a[n-1] then swap a[n-2] and a[n- 1]. Pass2. Step 1. if a[0]>a[1] then swap a[0] and a[1]. Step 2. if a[1]>a[2] then swap a[1] and a[2]. … Step n-2. if a[n-3]>a[n-2] then swap a[n-3] and a[n-2]. … Pass k. Step 1. if a[0]>a[1] then swap a[0] and a[1]. Step 2. if a[1]>a[2] then swap a[1] and a[2]. … Step n-k. if a[n-(k+1)]>a[n-k] then swap a[n-(k+1)] and a[n-k]. … Pass n-1 Step 1. if a[0]>a[1] then swap a[0] and a[1].

DOC-30-P13-Q61.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-30-P13-Q61.clean_question_text: What is insertion sort? Ans : This algorithm is very popular with bridge players when they sort their cards. In this procedure, we pick up a particular value and then insert it at the appropriate place in the sorted sub list.
DOC-30-P13-Q61.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-30-P13-Q61 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-30-P13-Q61.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-30-P13-Q61.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-30-P13-Q61.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-30-P13-Q61.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-30-P13-Q61.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-30-P13-Q61.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-30-P14-Q64.clean_question_text: What is the complexity of insertion sort? Ans : The worst-case performance occurs when the elements of the input array are in descending order. DOC-30-P17-Q71.family_title: Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run
DOC-30-P17-Q71.clean_question_text: What is the complexity of quicksort algorithm? Ans : Finding the location of the element that splits the array into two sections is an O(n) operation, because every element in the array is compared to the pivot element. After the division, each section is examined separately. If the array is split approximately in half (an optimistic assumption), then there will be log2ⁿ splits. Therefore, the total comparisons will be: f(n) = n*log2ⁿ = O(nlog2ⁿ)
DOC-30-P17-Q71.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-30-P17-Q71 (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
DOC-30-P17-Q71.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
DOC-30-P17-Q71.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-30-P17-Q71.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-30-P17-Q71.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-30-P17-Q71.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.

DOC-30-P18-Q75.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-30-P18-Q75.clean_question_text: What is the complexity of insertion sort? 
DOC-30-P18-Q75.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-30-P18-Q75 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-30-P18-Q75.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-30-P18-Q75.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-30-P18-Q75.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-30-P18-Q75.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-30-P18-Q75.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-30-P18-Q75.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-30-P19-Q78.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.

• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.

DOC-30-P20-Q80.time_complexity: O(n) linear time for Build-Max-Heap; O(log n) for Max-Heapify
DOC-30-P20-Q80.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-30-P20-Q80.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-30-P20-Q80.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-30-P20-Q80.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-30-P20-Q80.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-30-P21-Q85.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-30-P21-Q85 (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
DOC-30-P21-Q85.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
DOC-30-P21-Q85.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-30-P21-Q85.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-30-P21-Q85.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-30-P21-Q85.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-30-P21-Q85.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-30-P21-Q85.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-30-P23-Q95.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-30-P23-Q95.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-30-P23-Q95.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-28-P01-MCQ-Q01.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.

• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]

DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.clean_question_text: Which of the following operations on a queue implemented by an array in a naive way has time complexity O(n), where ‘n’ is the number of elements in the queue? (a) Enqueue (b) Dequeue (c) Push (d) isEmpty
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q20.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q25.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).

3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.

• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.

DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.clean_question_text: When does the worst case complexity happen for Insertion Sort? (a) When the array is already sorted (b) When the array is sorted in reverse order (c) When the array is not sorted (d) When the array is sorted till the midpoint and then reverse sorted
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-28-P04-MCQ-Q26.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-28-P05-MCQ-Q29.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-28-P05-MCQ-Q29.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-28-P05-MCQ-Q29.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-28-P05-MCQ-Q29.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-28-P05-MCQ-Q29.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).

• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q03.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q03.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-28-P05-SA-Q05.step_by_step_explanation:

3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q05.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q05.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q05.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.clean_question_text: The optimal data structure used to solve the Tower of Hanoi problem is _________.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06 (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q06.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

DOC-28-P05-SA-Q07.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q07.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q07.exam_ready_answer:

• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.

DOC-28-P05-SA-Q13.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q13.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.

• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q13.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-28-P05-SA-Q13.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-28-P06-LA-Q03.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.

5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q03.exam_ready_answer:

• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.

DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q04.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-28-P06-LA-Q10.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q10.step_by_step_explanation:

   - If operand: append directly to output.

• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.
DOC-28-P06-LA-Q10.common_mistakes: Treating ^ as left-associative instead of right-associative, or outputting '(' into the postfix string.

DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.clean_question_text: There are ‘n’ integers in a circular queue. We search for every ‘d’-th element starting from the queue beginning and mark it invalid. Starting from the first invalid element, this process continues, i.e., every ‘d’-th element is searched and marked invalid. Invalid items are no longer taken into account and skipped. That means if you come across an invalid item when you try to find the ‘d’-th element, you try the ‘d+1’-th element, if that is valid. If invalid, you try ‘d+2’-th element. DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q16.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.clean_question_text: The span of a stock’s price on a certain day, d, is the maximum number of consecutive days (up to the current day) the price of the stock has been less than or equal to its price on d. An example is give below: Day # 1 2 3 4 5 6 Price 9 3 5 2 7 12 Span 1 1 2 1 4 6 A naive comparison based algorithm will run in O(n²) time. You have to design an algorithm using stack so that the algorithm can be run in O(n) time. RECURSION
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-28-P07-LA-Q21.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.family_title: Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.clean_question_text: Write a small C function (no need for main, header files etc.) to print the moves of the well-known Tower of Hanoi problem using recursion. Assume that the smallest disc is numbered as ‘disc 1’ and the largest is ‘disc n’. Each of the three pegs is represented by a char (datatype): source (‘S’), destination (‘D’) and temporary (‘T’). Given below are some examples of the moves that you will print: Move the disc # 12 from T to D Move the disc # 4 from S to T. Now just write the output of your function if it is called with n = 4, where n is the number of discs.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24 (Tower of Hanoi: recursive algorithm, step-by-step move sequence, and recurrence)
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.exam_ready_answer:
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(1) = 1.
• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q24.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

DOC-28-P08-LA-Q26.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q26.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q26.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q26.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-28-P08-LA-Q26.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-28-P12-LA-Q66.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-28-P12-LA-Q66.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-28-P12-LA-Q66.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-28-P12-LA-Q66.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.

DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.time_complexity: Best Case: O(1), Worst Case: O(log n), Average Case: O(log n)
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.space_complexity: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive call stack
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.exam_ready_answer:
• Precondition: Input array must be strictly sorted.
• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q68.common_mistakes: Applying binary search on unsorted arrays, or using (low + high) / 2 without overflow guard.

DOC-28-P13-LA-Q74.direct_answer: Converted to Max-Heap by calling Max-Heapify from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q74.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Represent array elements as an implicit complete binary tree (1-based index: left child = 2i, right child = 2i + 1, parent = ⌊i/2⌋).
2. Identify last non-leaf node index = ⌊n/2⌋. Leaf nodes (⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n) trivially satisfy the heap property.
3. Loop i from ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1:
   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.
   - If swapped, recursively heapify the affected subtree.
4. Time Complexity is O(n) because nodes at height h cost O(h), and ∑ (h / 2^h) converges to 2.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q74.exam_ready_answer:
• Array Indexing (1-based): Parent = i/2, Left Child = 2i, Right Child = 2i + 1.
• Non-leaf nodes start from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1.
• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q74.common_mistakes: Iterating from 1 up to n instead of ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, or confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing.
DOC-28-P13-LA-Q74.beginner_notes: In 1-based array: left child is 2*i, right child is 2*i + 1. In 0-based: left is 2*i + 1, right is 2*i + 2.

DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q16.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q16.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.

• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q16.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q16.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q20.direct_answer: Pointer manipulation updating next links in-place.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q20.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Node definition: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; };
2. For Reversal: Use three pointers: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL.
3. Loop while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next; reverse link curr->next = prev; advance prev = curr; curr = next.
4. Update head = prev.
5. For Deletion of node X without head: Copy data from X->next into X, then delete X->next (X->next = X->next->next). Valid if X is not the last node.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q20.exam_ready_answer:
• Reversal requires 3 pointers: prev (NULL), curr (head), next (NULL).
• In-place update: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`
• Time Complexity: O(n), Space Complexity: O(1).
• Deleting node X without head pointer: Copy data of X->next to X, bypass X->next.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q20.common_mistakes: Losing the next node pointer before redirecting curr->next.
DOC-31-P03-PART1-Q20.beginner_notes: Always store `curr->next` in a temporary pointer before breaking the link.

DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.clean_question_text: The smallest element of an array’s index is called its (A) lower bound. (B) upper bound. (C) range. (D) extraction. 5
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-31-P04-PART1-Q27.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-31-P06-PART1-Q40.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-31-P06-PART1-Q40.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).

• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.

DOC-31-P08-PART1-Q50.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-31-P08-PART1-Q50.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-31-P08-PART1-Q50.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-31-P08-PART1-Q50.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-31-P08-PART1-Q50.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.clean_question_text: O(N) (linear time) is better than O(1) constant time. (A) True (B) False
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-31-P09-PART1-Q58.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.clean_question_text: Which sorting algorithm is best if the list is already sorted? Why?
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-31-P11-PART1-Q70.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q79.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q79.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q79.exam_ready_answer:

• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.

DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.clean_question_text: The largest element of an array index is called its (A) lower bound. (B) range. (C) upper bound. (D) All of these.
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-31-P13-PART1-Q81.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-31-P14-PART1-Q88.direct_answer: Divides sorted search interval in half by comparing key with middle element.
DOC-31-P14-PART1-Q88.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Precondition: Array MUST be sorted.
2. Initialize low = 0, high = n - 1.
3. While low ≤ high:
   - Calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (avoids integer overflow).
   - If arr[mid] == key: return mid (Found).
   - If arr[mid] < key: search right half, set low = mid + 1.
   - If arr[mid] > key: search left half, set high = mid - 1.
4. If low > high: return -1 (Not found).
5. Worst Case Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Solution: T(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
DOC-31-P14-PART1-Q88.exam_ready_answer:

• Recurrence Relation: T(n) = T(n/2) + c.
• Worst Case Time Complexity: ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 = O(log n).
• Mid calculation formula: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.

DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-31-P15-PART1-Q94.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.family_title: Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n)
DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.clean_question_text: Compare two functions 2 n and 4 2ⁿ for various values of n. Determine when second becomes larger than first. (5) When n=8, the value of n² and 2ⁿ/4 is same. Before that n² >2ⁿ/4, and after this value n²< 2ⁿ/4.
DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03 (Mathematical proofs of asymptotic bounds for given functions f(n))
DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P17-PART2-Q03.exam_ready_answer:

DOC-31-P19-PART2-Q07.direct_answer: Circular Queue wraps around indices using modulo arithmetic: (rear + 1) % MAX.
DOC-31-P19-PART2-Q07.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Front points to removal position; Rear points to last inserted position.
2. Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
3. Empty Condition: `front == -1` (or `front == rear` depending on convention).
4. Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; queue[rear] = item;` (if empty, `front = rear = 0`).
5. Dequeue: `item = queue[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = -1; else front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
6. Eliminates linear queue false overflow where rear reaches MAX-1 but front slots are empty.
DOC-31-P19-PART2-Q07.exam_ready_answer:
• Advantage over Linear Queue: Solves false overflow and memory wastage without shifting elements.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
• Complexity: O(1) time for both Enqueue and Dequeue.
DOC-31-P19-PART2-Q07.common_mistakes: Using standard rear++ which causes index out of bounds instead of `(rear + 1) % MAX`.
DOC-31-P19-PART2-Q07.beginner_notes: Modulo arithmetic `% MAX` acts like a clock: after 11 comes 12, then 1.

DOC-31-P28-PART2-Q16.direct_answer: Solved recursively by decomposing into moving n-1 disks to auxiliary rod.
DOC-31-P28-PART2-Q16.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Base Case: If n == 1, move disk 1 directly from Source to Destination rod.
2. Recursive Step:
   - Move top n - 1 disks from Source to Auxiliary (using Destination as helper).
   - Move disk n directly from Source to Destination.
   - Move n - 1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination (using Source as helper).
3. Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1.
4. Total moves = 2ⁿ - 1. For n=3: 7 moves; for n=4: 15 moves.

• Total Moves: 2ⁿ - 1 moves.
• Time Complexity: O(2ⁿ), Space Complexity: O(n) call stack.
• C Recursive function: TOH(n-1, from, aux, to); move disk n; TOH(n-1, aux, to, from);
DOC-31-P28-PART2-Q16.common_mistakes: Confusing the roles of destination and auxiliary pegs in the second recursive call.
DOC-31-P28-PART2-Q16.beginner_notes: Remember the rhythm: Source to Aux, Move Biggest, Aux to Destination.

3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).

• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.

DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-31-P35-PART2-Q24.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.family_title: Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.clean_question_text: Explain the method to calculate the address of an element in an array. A 4 25× matrix array DATA is stored in memory in ‘row-major order’. If base address is 200 and 4 = ω words per memory cell. Calculate the address of DATA [12, 3] . (8)
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35 (Row-major and Column-major 2D/multidimensional array element address calculation)
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.direct_answer: Calculated using Row-Major or Column-Major address calculation formula.
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Given array bounds: Row indices [L1 .. U1], Column indices [L2 .. U2].
2. Total rows R = U1 - L1 + 1, Total columns C = U2 - L2 + 1.
3. Row-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ].
4. Column-Major Address Formula: Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ].
5. Substitute base address, element size w bytes, and target indices (i, j) into the formula.
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.exam_ready_answer:
• Formula (Row-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (i - L1) · C + (j - L2) ]
• Formula (Column-Major): Addr(A[i][j]) = B + w · [ (j - L2) · R + (i - L1) ]
• Substitute given parameters and show intermediate multiplication and addition steps clearly.
• State final calculated memory address.
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.common_mistakes: Multiplying by R instead of C in row-major order, or forgetting base index L1/L2 when array is 1-indexed.
DOC-31-P41-PART2-Q35.beginner_notes: Row-major means you cross full rows first. Each full row has C elements.

DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q39.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:

   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.

DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q39.exam_ready_answer:
• Method: Use an operator stack based on operator precedence: () > ^ > *, / > +, -.
• Table of Execution: [Symbol Scanned, Stack Contents, Output Expression].
• Operands pass directly to output; operators wait on stack until lower precedence arrives.
• Final Postfix Expression is verified parenthesis-free.

DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40 (Quick Sort: Partitioning algorithms (Lomuto / Hoare), pivot selection, and dry run)
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.time_complexity: Divide-and-conquer partitioning (Complexity derivation excluded per syllabus)
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.space_complexity: O(log n) to O(n) call stack space
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.direct_answer: Partitions array around a pivot such that left elements ≤ pivot ≤ right elements.
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Select a pivot element (e.g. last element A[high] in Lomuto scheme).
2. Maintain partition index i starting at low - 1.
3. Scan j from low to high - 1: if A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i++ and swap A[i] with A[j].
4. Swap A[i + 1] with A[high] to place pivot in its permanent sorted location pi = i + 1.
5. Recursively invoke QuickSort on left subarray A[low .. pi - 1] and right subarray A[pi + 1 .. high].
6. NOTE: Complexity analysis derivation is explicitly excluded by the locked syllabus.
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.exam_ready_answer:
• Core Principle: Divide-and-conquer partitioning.
• Partition Procedure: Rearranges array so elements < pivot are left, elements > pivot are right.
• Pivot is permanently placed in its correct sorted position.
• Recursive calls sort the left and right partitions independently.
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.common_mistakes: Attempting full recurrence relations or worst-case derivations (which are excluded from syllabus!).
DOC-31-P43-PART2-Q40.beginner_notes: Once partitioned, the pivot never moves again.

DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.clean_question_text: How many key comparisons and assignments an insertion sort makes in its worst case? (4)
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-31-P44-PART2-Q41.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

   - Compare A[i] with left child A[2i] and right child A[2i+1].
   - Swap A[i] with largest child if child is greater.

• Max-Heapify compares node with its children and sinks down if smaller.
• Build-Max-Heap runs in O(n) linear time because most nodes are near the leaves with small heights.

DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.family_title: Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.clean_question_text: Describe insertion sort with a proper algorithm. What is the complexity of insertion sort in the worst case? (8)
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46 (Insertion Sort: algorithm, pass trace, and Best/Worst/Average case complexity analysis)
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.time_complexity: Best Case: O(n), Worst Case: O(n²), Average Case: O(n²)
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.direct_answer: Builds sorted prefix incrementally by inserting key element at correct position.
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Outer loop runs from i = 1 to n - 1.
2. Set key = arr[i], j = i - 1.
3. Shift all elements in arr[0..i-1] that are greater than key one position to the right: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) { arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j--; }
4. Insert key into vacant position: arr[j + 1] = key.
5. Best Case: Array already sorted. While loop condition fails on first check. (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts. Time = O(n).
6. Worst Case: Array reverse sorted. Element i shifts past all i elements. Total comparisons = ∑ i = n(n-1)/2. Time = O(n²).
7. Average Case: Each element compares against i/2 items on average. Total comparisons ≈ n(n-1)/4. Time = O(n²).
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.exam_ready_answer:
• Algorithm: In-place, stable comparison sort inserting key into sorted prefix.
• Best Case (Already Sorted): O(n) time, n-1 comparisons, 0 shifts.
• Worst Case (Reverse Sorted): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/2 comparisons and shifts.
• Average Case (Random): O(n²) time, n(n-1)/4 comparisons.
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.common_mistakes: Writing arr[j] >= key which breaks stability, or failing to state the exact summations for worst and average cases.
DOC-31-P47-PART2-Q46.beginner_notes: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand: take card i and slide it left into place.

DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.family_title: Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.clean_question_text: Why do we use a symptotic notation in the study of algorithm? Describe commonly used asymptotic notations and give their significance. (8) 50
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.solution_title: Complete Solution for DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50 (Formal definitions of Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations)
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.direct_answer: Big-O gives asymptotic upper bound, Big-Omega (Ω) gives lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) gives tight bound.
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
2. Big-Omega notation: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
3. Big-Theta notation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff ∃ constants c1 > 0, c2 > 0, n0 > 0 such that 0 ≤ c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
4. Example: For f(n) = 3n + 2, 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2, hence f(n) = O(n).
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.exam_ready_answer:
• Definition: Asymptotic notations describe the limiting behavior of an algorithm's running time as input size n approaches infinity.
• Big-O (Upper Bound): 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Ω (Lower Bound): 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Big-Θ (Tight Bound): c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
• Conclusion: Big-Theta indicates that g(n) is both an upper and lower bound within constant factors.
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.common_mistakes: Using negative constants c or failing to specify n0.
DOC-31-P49-PART2-Q50.beginner_notes: Think of Big-O as a ceiling and Big-Omega as a floor. If ceiling and floor match, you have Big-Theta.

DOC-31-P50-PART2-Q51.direct_answer: Converted by Shunting-Yard algorithm using an operator stack.
DOC-31-P50-PART2-Q51.step_by_step_explanation:
1. Initialize an empty operator stack and empty output string.
2. Scan infix expression from left to right:
   - If operand: append directly to output.
   - If '(': push onto stack.
   - If ')': pop and append to output until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
